Abstract.

Exponentials of (real/complex) vector fields are classically defined via the vector field integration. Take a 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra 𝕜⁡[x]⊂R⊂𝕜⁡[[x]],\Bbbk[x]\!\subset\!R\!\subset\!\Bbbk[\![x]\!], where 𝕜⊇ℚ\Bbbk\supseteq\mathbb{Q} is a local domain. Suppose a derivation ξ\xi is xx-adically nilpotent. Define the exp-operator via the Taylor expansion, eξ:=∑ξjj!.e^{\xi}:=\sum\frac{\xi^{j}}{j!}. It is a formal automorphism, eξ∈A​u​t𝕜​(𝕜⁡[[x]]).e^{\xi}\in Aut_{\Bbbk}(\Bbbk[\![x]\!]). When does eξe^{\xi} act on R​?R? When does the formal power series eξ​x∈𝕜⁡[[x]]e^{\xi}x\in\Bbbk[\![x]\!] belong to R​?R?

We address this question for the following rings.

  1. i.

    The algebraic power series, R=𝕜​⟨x⟩,R=\Bbbk\langle x\rangle, differentially finite (holonomic) power series, D⁡(𝕜⁡[x]),D(\Bbbk[x]), and their higher versions, Picard-Vessiot extensions D∙​(𝕜​[x]),D^{\bullet}(\Bbbk[x]), Picard-Vessiot closure D∞​(𝕜​[x]),D^{\infty}(\Bbbk[x]), and differentially-algebraic power series Da​l​g​(𝕜​[x]).D^{alg}(\Bbbk[x]).

  2. ii.

    Power series over normed fields. In particular, power series with coefficients of controlled growth, e.g. analytic/Denjoy-Carleman/Gevrey classes.

  3. iii.

    Germs of smooth functions C∞​(ℝn,o)/J,{\footnotesize\left.\raisebox{1.37775pt}{$C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n},o)$}\!/\!\raisebox{-1.37775pt}{$J$}\right.}, for arbitrary ideal J⊂C∞​(ℝn,o).J\!\subset\!C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n},o).

In case i. the operator eξe^{\xi} is transcendental, and the power series eξ​xe^{\xi}x is “usually” far from being algebraic. We give various criteria on eξ​xe^{\xi}x to belong to 𝕜​⟨x⟩,\Bbbk\langle x\rangle, D⁡(𝕜⁡[x]),D(\Bbbk[x]), D⁡(R),D(R), or Da​l​g​(𝕜​[x]).D^{alg}(\Bbbk[x]). Among our results are:

  • •

    the ring D∞​(𝕜​[x,y])D^{\infty}(\Bbbk[x,y]) does not admit the Weierstrass preparation theorem.

  • •

    (one variable case) If eξ​x∈D∞​(R),e^{\xi}x\in D^{\infty}(R), then eξ​x∈Rh​e​n​se^{\xi}x\in R^{hens} (the Henselization)

  • •

    (one variable polynomial case) eξ​x∈D∞​(𝕜⁡[x])e^{\xi}x\in D^{\infty}(\Bbbk[x]) if and only if ξ=c⋅xp⋅∂x,\xi=c\cdot x^{p}\cdot\partial_{x}, for some c∈𝕜.c\in\Bbbk.

In case ii. the answer is positive (i.e. eξe^{\xi} acts on RR) under rather weak assumptions on R.R.

In case iii. the answer is “totally negative”. For any ξ≠0\xi\neq 0 the operator eξe^{\xi} (defined as before) does not act on the quotients of the ring of germs of smooth functions, C∞​(ℝn,o)/J.{\footnotesize\left.\raisebox{1.37775pt}{$C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n},o)$}\!/\!\raisebox{-1.37775pt}{$J$}\right.}.

Key words and phrases: 
Derivations and their exponential map, transcendence, Picard-Vession extensions, linear ODE’s, Liouville type results, algebraic power series, differentially finite (holonomic) power series, differentially algebraic power series, Denjoy-Carleman/Gevrey classes.

1. Introduction

1.1.

Let 𝕜⊇ℚ\Bbbk\!\supseteq\!\mathbb{Q} be a local domain, e.g. a field. Let RR be a (not necessarily Noetherian) 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra satisfying: 𝕜⁡[x]⊂R⊆𝕜⁡[[x]].\Bbbk[x]\!\subset\!R\!\subseteq\!\Bbbk[\![x]\!]. We use multi-variables, x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}).

Take a 𝕜\Bbbk-linear derivation ξ∈Der𝕜⁡(R).\xi\in\Der_{\Bbbk}(R). For various purposes one needs “to integrate ξ\xi to a time-one flow”, i.e. to assign to ξ\xi the (𝕜\Bbbk-linear) automorphism of the algebra, eξ∈A​u​t𝕜​(R)e^{\xi}\in Aut_{\Bbbk}(R). In Differential Geometry (for 𝕜=ℝ,ℂ\Bbbk=\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}) the operator eξe^{\xi} is defined by vector field integration, resolving the system of ODE’s, x′=ξ⁡(x).x^{\prime}=\xi(x). For 𝕜⊇ℚ\Bbbk\supseteq\mathbb{Q} a local domain (with no norm) the natural definition is via the Taylor expansion, eξ:=∑j=0∞ξjj!.e^{\xi}\!:=\!\sum^{\infty}_{j=0}\frac{\xi^{j}}{j!}. The old question reads: When does eξe^{\xi} act on RR?

If R=𝕜⁡[x]R=\Bbbk[x] and ξ\xi is locally nilpotent11 1 i.e. for each f∈Rf\in R there exists N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} ensuring ξN​f=0\xi^{N}f=0, then one gets a well defined automorphism eξ↻R.e^{\xi}\circlearrowright R. These locally nilpotent derivations have been studied extensively, see e.g. [Freudenburg].

In local Geometry/Algebra, Singularity Theory, Dynamical Systems (and neighboring areas) one works with local 𝕜\Bbbk-algebras, 𝕜​[x](x)⊆R⊆𝕜⁡[[x]].\Bbbk[x]_{(x)}\!\subseteq\!R\!\subseteq\!\Bbbk[\![x]\!]. Then no (non-zero) derivation is locally nilpotent, see §2.1. If 𝕜\Bbbk has no pre-given topology, then even the coefficients of monomials in the power series eξ​fe^{\xi}f are not well defined. (They contain infinite summations.) Hence one restricts to “xx-adically nilpotent” derivations,

(1) Der𝕜n​i​l​p⁡(R):={ξ|ξN​(x)⊆(x)2​f​o​r​N≫1}⊂Der𝕜⁡(R).\Der^{nilp}_{\Bbbk}(R):=\{\xi\ |\ \xi^{N}(x)\!\subseteq\!(x)^{2}\ for\ N\gg 1\}\!\subset\!\Der_{\Bbbk}(R).

(And then ξN​(x)d⊆(x)d+1\xi^{N}(x)^{d}\!\subseteq\!(x)^{d+1} for each d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} and a corresponding N≫1N\gg 1.) Geometrically these are vector fields on (𝕜n,o)(\Bbbk^{n},o) that vanish at the origin and whose linear part is nilpotent.

This xx-adic nilpotence ensures (by the xx-adic completeness): eξe^{\xi} is a well-defined (formal) automorphism of the ring 𝕜⁡[[x]],\Bbbk[\![x]\!], [Bourbaki., Chapter II, §6]. Thus the initial question becomes: Does the action eξ↻𝕜⁡[[x]]e^{\xi}\circlearrowright\Bbbk[\![x]\!] restrict to the action eξ↻R​?e^{\xi}\circlearrowright R? The classical answers are:

  • •

    “yes” for the analytic ring 𝕜​{x},\Bbbk\{x\}, archimedean or non-archimedean, [Bourbaki., Chapter II,§7,§8]; “yes” for Gevrey classes, [Brochero.López];

  • •

    “almost never” for the ring of algebraic power series, 𝕜​⟨x⟩.\Bbbk\langle x\rangle. The power series eξ​xe^{\xi}x is typically non-algebraic, and was considered “completely transcendental”.

For other rings, 𝕜​[x](x)⊂R⊂𝕜⁡[[x]],\Bbbk[x]_{(x)}\!\subset\!R\!\subset\!\Bbbk[\![x]\!], only some particular (positive and negative) examples are known.

If ξ\xi acts on R,R, then, in particular, eξ​x∈R.e^{\xi}x\in R. The converse holds for rings admitting compositions, because eξ​f​(x)=f⁡(eξ​x)e^{\xi}f(x)=f(e^{\xi}x). Thus the essential question is whether eξ​x∈R,e^{\xi}x\in R, or “How far is the Lie series eξ​xe^{\xi}x from RR?”

For the rings like 𝕜​⟨x⟩,\Bbbk\langle x\rangle, D∙​(𝕜​[x])D^{\bullet}(\Bbbk[x]) this goes in the style of Liouville theory/Differential Galois theory, see e.g. [Raab-Singer] and [van der Put-Singer]. But the involved ODE, x′=ξ⁡(x),x^{\prime}=\xi(x), is non-linear. Thus the standard known results do not seem to be directly applicable.

1.2.

In the formal/analytic case the action eξ↻Re^{\xi}\circlearrowright R gives the Lie map Der𝕜n​i​l​p⁡(R)→e​x​pA​u​t𝕜​(R).\Der^{nilp}_{\Bbbk}(R)\ \lower 1.72218pt\hbox{$\mathrel{\mathop{\to}\limits^{\scriptscriptstyle{exp}}}$}\ Aut_{\Bbbk}(R). This allows to study the neighborhood of the unit element, I​d∈A​u​t𝕜​(R)Id\in Aut_{\Bbbk}(R), via the “tangent space to the group”, Der𝕜n​i​l​p⁡(R)\Der^{nilp}_{\Bbbk}(R), [Bourbaki., Chapter III]. Hence the importance of the exponentiability. More generally, these “Lie series of vector fields” are widespread in Mathematics and Physics, see e.g. [Olver], [Milnor], [Winkel]. In the analytic case they have been studied exhaustively through 20’th century.

In many cases eξ​x∉R,e^{\xi}x\not\in R, thus the map e​x​pexp is not defined on the whole module Der𝕜n​i​l​p⁡(R).\Der^{nilp}_{\Bbbk}(R). Then one asks more specific questions, dictated by applications.

  • •

    On which (largest) subset of Der𝕜n​i​l​p⁡(R)\Der^{nilp}_{\Bbbk}(R) is the map e​x​pexp defined? We call ξ\xi exponentiable over RR if eξ​x∈R.e^{\xi}x\in R. Denote the subset of exponentiable derivations by Der𝕜e​x​p⁡(R)⊆Der𝕜n​i​l​p⁡(R).\Der^{exp}_{\Bbbk}(R)\!\subseteq\!\Der^{nilp}_{\Bbbk}(R).

    A remark, if eξe^{\xi} acts on RR then so does ec⋅ξe^{c\cdot\xi} for any c∈𝕜,c\in\Bbbk, see Lemma 2.4. Thus the subset Der𝕜e​x​p⁡(R)⊆Der𝕜n​i​l​p⁡(R)\Der^{exp}_{\Bbbk}(R)\!\subseteq\!\Der^{nilp}_{\Bbbk}(R) is a 𝕜\Bbbk-cone. But it is often not a 𝕜\Bbbk-submodule.

  • •

    (The complexity of eξ​xe^{\xi}x for a given ξ\xi) Is eξ​xe^{\xi}x contained in a prescribed extension of R​?R? E.g. for DD-finite power series (and their higher analogs), can one ensure eξ​(Dj​(𝕜⁡[x]))⊆Dj+d​(𝕜⁡[x])e^{\xi}(D^{j}(\Bbbk[x]))\!\subseteq\!D^{j+d}(\Bbbk[x]) for some dd and j​?j? Or (at least) eξ​(Dj​(𝕜⁡[x]))⊆D∞​(𝕜⁡[x])​?e^{\xi}(D^{j}(\Bbbk[x]))\!\subseteq\!D^{\infty}(\Bbbk[x])?

  • •

    For many rings, even if eξe^{\xi} does not act on R,R, this operator is (x)(x)-adically approximated by automorphisms of R.R. This is frequently used for the study of the group A​u​t𝕜​(R)Aut_{\Bbbk}(R) in terms of the module Der𝕜⁡(R).\Der_{\Bbbk}(R). A more delicate question is: which derivations ξ∈Der𝕜n​i​l​p⁡(R)\xi\in\Der^{nilp}_{\Bbbk}(R) can be (x)(x)-adically approximated by exponentiable derivations? Namely: describe the (x)(x)-adic closure Der𝕜e​x​p⁡(R)¯⊆Der𝕜n​i​l​p⁡(R).\overline{\Der^{exp}_{\Bbbk}(R)}\!\subseteq\!\Der^{nilp}_{\Bbbk}(R).

    Suppose ξ\xi is (non)exponentiable, are its perturbations by terms of high enough orders (non) exponentiable? Is the property of being (non)exponentiable finitely determined?

  • •

    How to compute eξ​xe^{\xi}x effectively? Recall that eξ​xe^{\xi}x is the “time-one flow”, et​ξ​x|t=1,e^{t\xi}x|_{t=1}, for the (system of) ODE x′=ξ⁡(x).x^{\prime}=\xi(x). While the flow is transcendental in general, eξ​xe^{\xi}x has “neat formula” in some particular cases. E.g.

    (2) forξ=c⋅xp+1dd​x, with c∈𝕜 and p≥1, one has: eξx=x(1−c⋅p⋅xp)1p∈𝕜⟨x⟩.\text{for}\ \xi=c\cdot x^{p+1}\frac{d}{dx},\text{ with }c\in\Bbbk\text{ and }p\geq 1,\text{ one has: }e^{\xi}x=\frac{x}{\big(1-c\cdot p\cdot x^{p}\big)^{\frac{1}{p}}}\in\Bbbk\langle x\rangle.

    This classical formula is widely used in Mathematis and Physics, e.g. [Milnor], [Olver], [Schottenloher]. More generally, one needs a closed formula for eξ​xe^{\xi}x in terms of some “finite elementary operations”, e.g. algebraic extensions, antiderivatives, and resolving implicit function equations.

We address these questions for the three (most important) classes of rings of the abstract.

1.3. The results

The standard starting point is: exponentiability vs solvability of ODE’s.
Lemma ​2.4 ​(roughly) eξ​x∈Re^{\xi}x\!\in\!R if and only if the ODE-system x′=ξ⁡(x)x^{\prime}\!=\!\xi(x) is solvable over R.R.

Hence the initial question becomes: “Is RR ODE-closed?” Or, for which systems of ODE’s over RR the (unique, formal) solution belongs to R​?R?

This question was studied for some subrings of the ring C∞​(𝒰)C^{\infty}(\mathcal{U}) of smooth functions, see e.g. [Rainer-Schindl.16]. Many results are known for Gevrey classes, see [Cano] and references therein.

1.3.1. The one-variable case, n=1,n=1, and the rings 𝕜​⟨x⟩,\Bbbk\langle x\rangle, Dj​(𝕜​[x]),D^{j}(\Bbbk[x]), D∞​(𝕜​[x]),D^{\infty}(\Bbbk[x]), Da​l​g​(𝕜​[x])D^{alg}(\Bbbk[x])

(See §2.3 for the definitions.) Recall that eξ​xe^{\xi}x is the time-one flow of the vector field ξ.\xi. Therefore eξ​xe^{\xi}x can be computed by resolving the ODE x′=ξ⁡(x).x^{\prime}=\xi(x). This ODE is integrated (in the completely standard way) to get the implicit function equation:

Lemma 3.1. 1. The power series y⁡(x)=eξ​x∈𝕜⁡[[x]]y(x)=e^{\xi}x\in\Bbbk[\![x]\!] is determined by the equation

(3) 1c⋅a​(y)p−1c⋅a​(x)p+r​e​so​ω⋅l​n​yx=1.\frac{1}{c\cdot a(y)^{p}}-\frac{1}{c\cdot a(x)^{p}}+res_{o}\omega\cdot ln\frac{y}{x}=1.

(Here r​e​so​ωres_{o}\omega is the residue of the associated 1-form.)

2. In particular, if r​e​so​ω=0res_{o}\omega\!=\!0 then eξ​x=a−1​[a⁡(x)(1+c⋅a​(x)p)1p].e^{\xi}x\!=\!a^{-1}[\frac{a(x)}{\big(1+c\cdot a(x)^{p}\big)^{\frac{1}{p}}}].

Here a−1​[…]a^{-1}[\dots] is the inverse of the power series a⁡(x)a(x).

Thus eξ​xe^{\xi}x is not “arbitrarily complicated”, but belongs to a controlled extension of the initial ring R.R. This has numerous consequences.

  • •

    In several “numerical cases” we have neat formulas, with eξ​x∈D2​(𝕜⁡[x]),e^{\xi}x\in D^{2}(\Bbbk[x]), see Example 3.2. But immediately we hit the nasty case:
    Example 3.3. eξ​x∉D∞​(𝕜⁡[x])e^{\xi}x\not\in D^{\infty}(\Bbbk[x]) for ξ=−x2​e−xx−1∂x.\xi=-\frac{x^{2}e^{-x}}{x-1}\partial_{x}.
    This shows how complicated the power series eξ​xe^{\xi}x can be, even if we start from x2​e−x1+x∈D1​(𝕜⁡[x]).\frac{x^{2}e^{-x}}{1+x}\!\in\!D^{1}(\Bbbk[x]). (Recall that D∞​(𝕜​[x])D^{\infty}(\Bbbk[x]) is the Picard-Vessiot closure of 𝕜⁡[x]\Bbbk[x] inside 𝕜⁡[[x]]\Bbbk[\![x]\!].)

  • •

    An offshoot of this nasty case is the pathology of the Picard-Vessiot closure:
    Corollary 3.5. The ring D∞​(𝕜​[x,y]),D^{\infty}(\Bbbk[x,y]), being regular, local, Henselian, does not admit the Weierstrass preparation theorem. (In particular, D∞​(𝕜​[x¯])D^{\infty}(\Bbbk[\underline{x}]) is not a W-system.)

    This (unpleasant) result seems to be new. Examples of regular local Henselian rings with no Weierstrass preparation are known in Analysis e.g. Gevrey or quasi-analytic Denjoy-Carleman rings for n≥2,n\geq 2, [A.B.B.N.Z.], [Parus.Rol.]. But the ring D∞​(𝕜​[x,y])D^{\infty}(\Bbbk[x,y]) is the first “purely algebraic” case, over arbitrary field 𝕜.\Bbbk.

  • •

    For the much larger ring of differentially algebraic power series the statement is positive (and probably known):
    Corollary 3.6. 1. eξ​x∈Da​l​g​(𝕜⁡[x])e^{\xi}x\in D^{alg}(\Bbbk[x]) for any ξ∈Dern​i​l​p⁡(Da​l​g​(𝕜⁡[x])).\xi\in\Der^{nilp}(D^{alg}(\Bbbk[x])).
    2. For algebraic derivations, ξ∈Der𝕜n​i​l​p⁡(𝕜⁡⟨x⟩),\xi\in\Der_{\Bbbk}^{nilp}(\Bbbk\langle x\rangle), the differential order of eξ​xe^{\xi}x is 1.

  • •

    Another application of Lemma 3.1 is the density result:
    Corollary 3.7. The (x)(x)-adic closure of the set of exponentiable derivations, Der𝕜e​x​p⁡(𝕜⁡⟨x⟩)¯⊂Der𝕜n​i​l​p⁡(𝕜⁡[[x]]),\overline{\Der^{exp}_{\Bbbk}(\Bbbk\langle x\rangle)}\!\subset\!\Der_{\Bbbk}^{nilp}(\Bbbk[\![x]\!]), is defined by the single condition, r​e​so​ω=0.res_{o}\omega=0.

The natural goal (in view of §1.2) is: assuming eξ​x∈D⁡(R),e^{\xi}x\!\in\!D(R), for a subring R⊂𝕜⁡[[x]],R\!\subset\!\Bbbk[\![x]\!], to push eξ​xe^{\xi}x “closer to RR”. For algebraic power series, ξ∈Der𝕜n​i​l​p⁡(𝕜⁡⟨x⟩),\xi\!\in\!\Der^{nilp}_{\Bbbk}(\Bbbk\langle x\rangle), we get a strong criterion:
Theorem 3.9. If eξ​x∈D∞​(R)e^{\xi}x\in D^{\infty}(R) then eξ​x∈Rh​e​n​s.e^{\xi}x\in R^{hens}. (The Henselization of R.R.)
Corollary 3.10. In particular, eξ​x∈D∞​(𝕜⁡[x])e^{\xi}x\in D^{\infty}(\Bbbk[x]) if and only if eξ​x∈𝕜​⟨x⟩.e^{\xi}x\in\Bbbk\langle x\rangle.

This (completely new) Liouville-type dichotomy can be stated as “the operator eξe^{\xi} is orthogonal to the hierarchy D1​(R)⊂D2​(R)⊂⋯D^{1}(R)\!\subset\!D^{2}(R)\!\subset\!\cdots”.

For polynomial derivations the result is even stronger, showing that (2) is the only case with a D∞D^{\infty}-answer:
Theorem 3.11. Let ξ=a(x)⋅∂x\xi=a(x)\cdot\partial_{x} with a⁡(x)∈(x)2⊂𝕜⁡[x].a(x)\in(x)^{2}\!\subset\!\Bbbk[x]. Then eξ​x∈D∞​(𝕜⁡[x])e^{\xi}x\in D^{\infty}(\Bbbk[x]) if and only if ξ=c⋅xp⋅∂x,\xi=c\cdot x^{p}\cdot\partial_{x}, for some c∈𝕜.c\in\Bbbk.

1.3.2. The case of several variables, n≥2n\geq 2

Here the study of eξ​xe^{\xi}x is as complicated as the solution of systems of (arbitrary, nonlinear) ODE’s. Here enter the difficulties of first integrals. In §3.5 we give explicit formulas only for derivations with “separable variables”. (In this case one has immediate full system of first integrals.)

1.3.3. Power series in nn variables, with coefficients in a normed field.

Here derivations are exponentiable under rather weak assumptions. Let 𝕜⁡[x]⊂R⊂𝕜⁡[[x]],\Bbbk[x]\!\subset\!R\!\subset\!\Bbbk[\![x]\!], where 𝕜\Bbbk is a normed field.

Theorem 4.1. Suppose RR is “closed under majorization of coefficients”, and satisfies the “implicit function theorem in two variables”. Then eξ​x∈Re^{\xi}x\in R for any ξ∈Der𝕜n​i​l​p⁡(R).\xi\in\Der^{nilp}_{\Bbbk}(R).

The proof goes by reduction to the one-variable case (n=1n\!=\!1). Then we invoke Lemma 3.1.

In the simplest case of analytic power series, 𝕜​{x},\Bbbk\{x\}, we get the classical Cauchy theorem for analytic flows of vector fields (over arbitrary normed field, e.g. p-adics). Unlike the numerous proofs of that Cauchy theorem, e.g. see the references in [Carrillo], ours does not involve any bounds or estimates.

More interesting cases for Theorem 4.1 are rings with coefficients of controlled growth, e.g. Denjoy-Carleman and Gevrey classes, Example 4.2.

1.3.4. Smooth function germs.

For the ring R=C∞​(ℝn,o)/J,R={\footnotesize\left.\raisebox{1.37775pt}{$C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n},o)$}\!/\!\raisebox{-1.37775pt}{$J$}\right.}, assuming the zero locus of JJ is not just the origin o∈ℝn,o\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, the answer is totally negative.
Theorem 5.1. For any derivation ≠ξ∈Derℝ⁡(R)0\!\neq\!\xi\!\in\!\Der_{\mathbb{R}}(R) the operator eξe^{\xi} does not act on R.R.

Namely, for any given ξ\xi we construct a function-germ f∈C∞​(ℝn,o)f\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n},o) such that eξ​fe^{\xi}f diverges on a convergent sequence of points o←{z∙}⊂V⁡(J)o\leftarrow\{z_{\bullet}\}\!\subset\!V(J).

This shows (again) how complicated is the ring C∞​(ℝn,o),C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n},o), as compared to various subrings of 𝕜⁡[[x]].\Bbbk[\![x]\!].

The proof is of (quite non-algebraic) C∞C^{\infty}-nature. The statement is immediate when ξ|o≠0.\xi|_{o}\neq 0. (Then ξ\xi can be rectified, and one invokes Borel’s lemma.) But the case of ξ|o=0\xi|_{o}=0 is completely non-trivial.

1.3.5. The further work

These results are just the peak of the iceberg. The operator eξe^{\xi} is the common/widespread tool in Mathematics and Physics, hence every property is of immediate value.
Our methods are applicable to various other rings, e.g. the traditional rings of Transcendence Theory and Diophantine Approximations (or Analytic Combinatorics), Mahler functions, G-functions, E-functions. Some of our results extend naturally to the case of n≥2.n\geq 2.

All this stuff is postponed to the subsequent paper.

  1. i.

    As one sees from the proof, eξe^{\xi} does not act on any subring R⊆C∞​(ℝn,o)R\!\subseteq\!C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n},o) that contains enough flat functions with fast growing derivatives.

Then for any (x)(x)-adically nilpotent derivation ξ∈Derℝn​i​l​p⁡(R)\xi\in\Der^{nilp}_{\mathbb{R}}(R) the operator eξe^{\xi} acts on RR. Indeed, in this case Borel’s lemma ensures the isomorphism:

    (49) C∞​(ℝn,o)/J≅C∞​(ℝn,o)/𝔪∞​╱​J⋅C∞​(ℝn,o)/𝔪∞→∼ℝ⁡[[x¯]]​╱​J⋅C∞​(ℝn,o)/𝔪∞.{\footnotesize\left.\raisebox{1.37775pt}{$C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n},o)$}\!/\!\raisebox{-1.37775pt}{$J$}\right.}\cong{\footnotesize\left.\raisebox{4.13332pt}{$C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n},o)/{\mathfrak{m}}^{\infty}$}\!\!\diagup\!\!\raisebox{-4.13332pt}{$J\cdot{\footnotesize\left.\raisebox{1.37775pt}{$C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n},o)$}\!/\!\raisebox{-1.37775pt}{${\mathfrak{m}}^{\infty}$}\right.}$}\right.}\xrightarrow[\,\smash{\raisebox{3.46594pt}{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}\,]{}{\footnotesize\left.\raisebox{4.13332pt}{$\mathbb{R}[\![\underline{x}]\!]$}\!\!\diagup\!\!\raisebox{-4.13332pt}{$J\cdot{\footnotesize\left.\raisebox{1.37775pt}{$C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n},o)$}\!/\!\raisebox{-1.37775pt}{${\mathfrak{m}}^{\infty}$}\right.}$}\right.}.

    And we observe that the ring ℝ⁡[[x¯]]​╱​J⋅C∞​(ℝn,o)/𝔪∞{\footnotesize\left.\raisebox{4.13332pt}{$\mathbb{R}[\![\underline{x}]\!]$}\!\!\diagup\!\!\raisebox{-4.13332pt}{$J\cdot{\footnotesize\left.\raisebox{1.37775pt}{$C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n},o)$}\!/\!\raisebox{-1.37775pt}{${\mathfrak{m}}^{\infty}$}\right.}$}\right.} is 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}}-complete.
